description:
Snoopy’s O2: because every astronaut deserves someone watching over their heartbeat.

When an astronaut leaves Earth, they leave behind hospitals and familiar faces. We want to build the software that takes their place: a health monitoring system that watches over them, spots trouble early, and tells the crew and mission control what matters, simply and clearly.
Ready to keep every heartbeat nominal, even in zero gravity? Join Snoopy’s O2.
summary: From Mars, a message to Earth takes up to 22 minutes each way, so a reply from the medical crew can take 44 minutes or more. Until help arrives, astronauts have to be their own first doctor. SAGE (Self-Assessment Guide for Explorers) is an offline, two-minute daily health check that learns each astronaut's own normal and builds the astronaut’s own twin for each flight day. As per NASA’s data, nausea on flight day 2 is expected; the same nausea on day 10 with a higher heart rate and 5 hours of sleep is not, so SAGE treats them differently. After each check, SAGE analyses and adjusts its responses to the four questions: Do I need to act? Is this normal for space? Can I trust the reading? Can I trust how I feel? It then gives one of four levels (Routine, Recheck, Contact medical crew, Urgent), possible causes with sources, and a ready summary for the medical crew completely offline. We tested it on 894 real NASA Inspiration4 blood measurements: SAGE's 95% range held 93.8% of real return-day values, against 71.1% for a personal baseline alone, and alerts fell from 37 to 8.
details:
Problem:
From Mars, a message to Earth takes up to 22 minutes each way, so a reply from the medical crew can take 44 minutes or more. Until help arrives, astronauts have to be their own first doctor.

• Normal space changes look like illness. For instance, up to about 70% of astronauts get space sickness early in flight, and ISS crews have an average of 6.09 hours of sleep and have lower blood pressure. Earth’s scales flag these expected changes as medical issues, which causes false alarms, wastes time and erodes trust. The reverse also happens: a reading inside Earth's normal range can hide a real change for that person.

• One person’s large change can hide inside the expected range for the entire population.

• Numbers alone don’t tell anything about what to do. Astronauts need to know whether to act, why it might be happening and what to do next. The medical crew needs to see the priority list in which astronauts require medical support.

Solution: SAGE
SAGE is an offline digital health twin for the two gaps in space medicine: late help from Earth, and Earth’s health ranges that get space wrong. A Bayesian model learns each astronaut’s personal normal and adjusts it for each flight day using real NASA astronaut data. In 2 minutes, it gives a clear answer, its possible causes and the next step.

• Learns your normal: after 3 calm checks, every reading is compared with the astronaut’s own usual along with the change expected on that flight day. A Bayesian model, built from published research and NASA resources, adjusts this space-normal range.

• Answers four questions: Do I need to act? Is this normal for space? Can I trust the reading? Can I trust how I feel?

• Gives one clear level: Routine, Recheck, Contact medical crew or Urgent. Each comes with possible causes and sources, what to do now, and a readable and complete summary for the medical crew.

• Checks the mind too: It considers daily mood and alertness ratings, four short mood questions each week and a reaction game that are compared with the astronaut’s own normal, so SAGE can spot when they perform worse than they feel.

Also included:

•            A 3D body twin with 13 organ reports

•            Radiation estimates by location and an approximate bone-loss estimate

•            Trends, points and patches, and a Learn library

•            Live NASA ISS cabin CO₂ and NASA solar-storm alerts

•            A medical-crew view that sorts the whole crew by urgency

•            Works fully offline, and data stays on the device

Evidence:
We tested SAGE on 894 real blood measurements from the four Inspiration4 astronauts (NASA OSD-569, OSD-575). Each astronaut was left out in turn: the model learned from the other three and predicted the missing astronaut’s return-day values, giving 128 predictions.

• SAGE’s 95% range held 93.8% of real return-day values, against 71.1% for a personal baseline alone.

• Flags after landing fell from 37 to 8 of 128.

• False alarms before launch fell from 39 to 20 of 128.

The code, every prediction, and resource validations are public on GitHub.

Impact:

• Astronaut: They get a clear answer in 2 minutes, even offline.

• Medical crew: They see everyone in a single place, with the most urgent first, with alerts, trends and analysis

• Earth: SAGE could help get responses and help from Antarctic stations, ships at sea and remote clinics.

Next steps:
A doctor’s review of the clinical rules, a week of checks with real users, and importing data from wearables.

Limits:

• SAGE is not a diagnosis or a medical device.

• Tested and trained on data from 4 astronauts

• Radiation and organ data come mostly from animal studies, and Moon and Mars bone-loss rates are scaled from a mouse study

Built with:

•            Languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python

•            Libraries: three.js 0.160.0 (3D body model), Lightstreamer Web Client 9.2.3 (live ISS cabin CO₂), esbuild 0.28.2 (offline build), Node.js (tests), Python standard library (model and validation)

•            NASA data: NASA OSDR (OSD-569, OSD-575, ISS dosimetry), NASA DONKI, NASA ISS Live, NASA-STD-3001, NASA Human Research Program

•            Tools: GitHub, Netlify (hosting), Visual Studio Code

Use of AI:
We used Claude (Anthropic) to get help and debug much of the app and, to help find research sources, and to help draft text and slides. We came up with the idea and made all final decisions. We reviewed and tested all AI-assisted work ourselves.
